live in the suburbs” — Tracy Chapman</em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em>“Outside suburbia’s sprawling everywhere/ I don’t want to go, baby” — Kim Wilde</em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I grew up in the suburbs, and when I got the chance, I moved to a big city and never looked back.</span><span class="footnote-anchor-email" data-component-name="FootnoteAnchorToDOMStatic" style="font-size: 20px;">¹</span><span> I love living in dense, built-up urban areas, with great train systems and tons of restaurants and shops. Japanese cities are the best in the world, and I’ve </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/971bb0b8-4e5a-466f-8365-61ae940e6282?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">written</a><span> plenty of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cb5f6f8e-42f0-4dbe-83b4-fa9f056c4100?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">posts</a><span> about </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/661b356f-d594-4ff4-8c87-6dac07e8128d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">what makes</a><span> them </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0ee8ca4a-a322-459e-8b90-69ed490cda76?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">so great</a><span>. But you don’t have to be Japan in order to create amazing metropolises — New York City, Paris, Istanbul, Seoul, London, etc. are all excellent places to live. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I’m far from the only person who feels this way. Rents in New York City are </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a6e74fcf-04b0-4f02-b78e-f4268c16a710?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">absolutely insane</a><span> — $5300 a month to live in Manhattan, $4350 to live in Brooklyn. That’s partly because there are a lot of good jobs in NYC — it’s a cluster for industries like finance and media. But more and more, Americans move to cities because they </span><em>like living there</em><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As early as 2000, economists were </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/01952ad9-8f12-43a9-a034-3de96c451eb5?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">starting to find</a><span> that “amenities” were driving America’s urban revival even more than job opportunities were. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/22de1303-9410-4a56-9068-b618544a5235?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Couture and Handbury (2020)</a><span> find that wanting to be close to restaurants and nightlife explains about 40% of the trend of young, high-earning, college-educated people</span><span class="footnote-anchor-email" data-component-name="FootnoteAnchorToDOMStatic" style="font-size: 20px;">²</span><span> moving to cities in recent decades. Furthermore, the stereotype of dense cities as crime-ridden and unsafe is just wrong — NYC has </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f4862068-87d7-4eba-b6bd-24897cd4b494?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">one of the lowest violent crime rates</a><span> among big cities in America.  </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I’ve been </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/191288dc-6bda-444e-90f3-b1fd1fbeec83?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">a relentless advocate</a><span> of building more dense, walkable cities in America. Not only would this raise GDP (because of improved clustering effects), but it would let Americans live where they want. The demand for life in cities like NYC exceeds America’s willingness to supply these environments; this raises rents in places like NYC, which pushes a lot of people into the suburbs who don’t want to be there. Forcing those city types into the ‘burbs raises rents for people who </span><em>like </em><span>suburbia. Basically, everyone would be happy if America had a few more Manhattans and a lot more Brooklyns.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Yet among my fellow urbanists and YIMBYs, I often encounter disdain or outright hostility toward the suburbs that define most of America’s present urban landscape. This isn’t just an urbanist thing, of course — my own parents had a lot of negative things to say about suburbia, and ranting against its sterility and boredom is a staple of pop culture. But the criticisms are just way overdone; the suburbs are not the isolating, lonely hell that they’re often made out to be. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And I think that the constant ranting against the suburbs complicates the quest for denser cities. It creates the suspicion that urbanists and YIMBYs want to make the whole nation into Manhattan. Nothing like that could ever happen, of course; even Japan is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9ada3930-d97e-424f-9f52-a153ceb9a988?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">mostly suburbanized</a><span>. But painting the quest for denser metropolises as an attack on suburbia makes everything needlessly confrontational, polarized, and zero-sum. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So I think it’s helpful to go through some reasons why the suburbs aren’t actually as bad as they say. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" red arrow by Noah Smith</span></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Why do Americans take less time to commute to work? One reason is that it’s not just our </span><em>homes </em><span>that are scattered and dispersed; our </span><em>workplaces </em><span>are too. America’s urban agglomerations are </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8db83ce4-aefe-427c-8af5-a256bd0e1324?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">polycentric</a><span>; they’re not just one central business district surrounded by concentric rings of houses. Suburbanites tend to live near where they work. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Another reason Americans have shorter commutes is that </span><em>cars are almost always faster than public transit</em><span> at getting you from point A to point B. This isn’t just </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/455effee-f1a8-46b1-b7d1-02759f735f27?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">true in places like America and Canada</a><span> that are built with cars in mind. It’s true in places like Stockholm and Amsterdam that were built to be transit-friendly — even when you take parking time into account. In fact, it’s not even close. This is from “Disparities in travel times between car and transit: Spatiotemporal patterns in cities”, by </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5a884076-62da-48ea-9cde-369aa7b28f9d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Liao et al. (2020)</a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We use real-world data to make realistic estimates of travel time by car and by PT [Public Transit] and compare their performance by time of day and by travel distance across cities. Our results suggest that using PT takes on average 1.4–2.6 times longer than driving a car. The share of area where travel time favours PT over car use is very small: 0.62% (0.65%), 0.44% (0.48%), 1.10% (1.22%) and 1.16% (1.19%) for the daily average (and during peak hours) for São Paulo, Sydney, </span><strong>Stockholm</strong><span>, and </span><strong>Amsterdam</strong><span>, respectively…A systematic comparison between these two modes shows that the average travel time disparity is surprisingly similar across cities…for travel distances less than 3 km, then increases rapidly but quickly stabilises at around 2. [emphasis mine]</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And here’s a chart, showing that public transit takes more time whether (2020)</a></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That doesn’t mean cars are </span><em>better </em><span>than public transit. Cars cost more, and they require a lot more land to move the same number of people. But because they take you directly from point to point, instead of making a circuit and stopping periodically, they get you there faster. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Of course, commuting by car and commuting by train or bus aren’t the same experience. Driving gives you more privacy, but it forces you to pay attention to the road instead of reading or playing games. Traffic can be frustrating, but so can jostling and bumping strangers for a space on the train. You’re a lot less likely to be sexually harassed in your car, but you’re more likely to die in an accident than to be murdered on the bus. And so on.</span><span class="footnote-anchor-email" data-component-name="FootnoteAnchorToDOMStatic" style="font-size: 20px;">³</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But the point is, cars are not a cost forced upon suburbanites in exchange for their large houses, as </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2ecb8f0b-91b3-4f7b-9185-454ced918eaf?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">some urbanists believe</a><span>. They are a thing people want in and of themselves, and are willing to pay a lot of money for, all over the world. The convenience, sense of freedom, and privacy cars offer is a </span><em>benefit </em><span>of suburbia to many people, in addition to the large house and cheap land. Car ownership is a form of wealth. </span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">The suburbs are not lonely and isolating</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Again and again, I hear urbanists declare that the suburbs are lonely and isolating. It certainly sounds logical. In a city, you’re walking past other people constantly — on the street, on the train, in cafes and restaurants. In suburbia, you’re shut at home inside your giant house or alone in the metal shell of your car. How could suburbia </span><em>not </em><span>be more lonely than the big city? </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But in survey after survey, we don’t find this to be the case. Here’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8091a68c-aece-4796-baf8-f08c39b8d822?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Abshire et al. (2022)</a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Data were obtained from 616 adults (278 from small rural, 100 from large rural, 98 from suburban, and 140 from urban areas) from June 2018 through October 2019…Mean unadjusted loneliness scores were lower in suburban compared to urban areas…The prevalence of loneliness was 50.7%, 59.0%, </span><strong>40.8%</strong><span>, and 54.3% in small rural, large rural, suburban, and urban areas, respectively. </span><strong>Suburban living was associated with lower odds for being lonely compared to urban living</strong><span>…but this association was not statistically significant in the adjusted model[.] [emphasis mine]</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And here’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b17eac35-3106-4997-ae91-cc10039a55c8?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Hammond et al. (2021)</a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Data from 756 participants who completed 16,602 assessments between April 2018 and March 2020 were used in order to investigate associations between momentary feeling of loneliness, the social environment (i.e. overcrowding, social inclusivity, population density) and the built environment (i.e. contact with nature)…</span><strong>Increased overcrowding and population density were associated with higher levels of loneliness</strong><span>; in contrast, social inclusivity and contact with nature were associated with lower levels of loneliness. These associations remained significant after adjusting for age, gender, ethnicity, education and occupation. [emphasis mine]</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And here’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5e396d40-2408-4113-a07e-92ee2273b7ea?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Morris and Pfeiffer (2016)</a><span>: </span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Based on data from the 2003 to 2013 American Time Use Surveys, this research…assess[es] whether suburban living is associated with less socializing than city living in mid-to-large American metropolitan areas. After controlling for personal characteristics, we find </span><strong><span>no meaningful difference in suburbanites’ and city dwellers’ time spent socializing</span></strong><span> across a wide range of social activities. [emphasis mine]</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8e5f2432-befe-45f4-b2d5-30947b0938c3?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Bower et al. (2022)</a><span> review 57 different studies and find no systematic association between loneliness and any measurable feature of the built environment.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Why doesn’t the simple intuition work here? Probably because people aren’t just like particles bouncing around in a chemistry experiment — they don’t simply form human connections and bonds just because they happen to walk past each other. A few relationships form from random urban conversations, but most form through work, or friends-of-friends, or shared hobbies, etc. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And while meeting a ton of new people is fun, what really gets rid of loneliness is repeated interaction with people you know and care about. Imagine going to ten parties filled with strangers versus having two close friends over for dinner. Which of those is more likely to leave you feeling lonely? What about 100 Hinge dates versus having a relationship? Remember that Japan has the world’s best cities, but struggles with widespread loneliness.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In fact, suburbs have some features that make it </span><em>easier</em><span> to interact with the people you really care about. Those big houses aren’t just for walking around all alone and going “Wow my house is so huge”. They’re for </span><em>entertaining guests</em><span>. It’s harder to have a dinner party or a TV night or a game night at a tiny little Manhattan apartment than at a big suburban McMansion. Cars help too; those short travel times make it easier to just pop over and hang. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This doesn’t mean cities are socially inferior to suburbs. Constantly meeting new people is exciting. There’s more fun stuff to go out and do with your friends in a city — restaurants, parties, and so on. It’s just a different lifestyle. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">There’s a reason people are moving to the ‘burbs</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The urban revival of the 1990s through the 2010s was </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e5b758ad-7351-4ed9-8e49-722d31b2302c?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">a modest thing</a><span>. It was </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cc503d9c-54b2-4425-8994-98081efea70c?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">largely driven</a><span> by young people, high earners, and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/22de1303-9410-4a56-9068-b618544a5235?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">educated people</a><span>. shows</a><span> that although the densest city centers are rebounding from the pandemic, more than 100% of this is driven by immigration — domestic migration is still strongly away from city centers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In fact, the new suburbanization trend is being led by Millennials. This is from </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/39b33ac1-10d2-4a3e-b6f9-72d21c86f32d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the Joint Center for Housing Studies</a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>[W]e found that throughout the past decade millennials were moving to suburbs that were farther out from the city center. There are many </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f6f8a784-371e-4b99-be55-21b3703c6572?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">ways to define suburbs</a><span>, and in this paper </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d84d9905-79d2-4e84-800b-ec08941a9a72?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">we rely on a framework</a><span> that considers rates of homeownership, single-family housing, and car commuting, in addition to proximity to a metro’s urban core. While there is extensive </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8289fbcd-9b25-4870-abfb-ebf73f9bc742?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">research</a><span> and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d5f2e0a9-928d-443f-8488-7fe3f461ee9d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">discussion</a><span> about millennial preferences for walkable urban areas, we found that </span><strong><span>the places with the largest increases of early millennials were both suburban and on the periphery of metropolitan areas</span></strong><span>. [emphasis mine]</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Why are Millennials moving out? Part of it — the part that urbanists and YIMBYs will emphasize — is that they’re being </span><em>pushed </em><span>out by higher rents, which are a result of cities failing to build more housing. But that’s not the whole story. Millennials are also being pulled to the suburbs, because suburbs are generally </span><em>better for raising kids</em><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a55f4f49-4ab8-48f2-89f1-b09298a11a53?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Albouy and Faberman (2025)</a><span> find that the kind of high-skilled workers who drove the urban boomlet of the 1990s through the 2010s tend to move out — and value urban amenities less — once they get a little older:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We show that high-skill workers disproportionately sort into high-amenity areas, but do so </span><strong>relatively early in life</strong><span>. Workers of all skill levels </span><strong>tend to move towards lower-amenity areas during their thirties and forties</strong><span>. Consequently, individuals’ time use and expenditures on activities related to local amenities are U-shaped over the life cycle…We present evidence that the move towards lower-amenity (and lower-cost) metropolitan areas is driven by changes in the number of household children over the life cycle: individuals, particularly the college educated, tend to </span><strong>move towards lower-amenity areas after having their first child</strong><span>. [emphasis mine]</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Kolko shows something similar — people with a kid over 6 tended to move out Kolko</a></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Anyone with kids can easily rattle off the reasons why suburbs make it easier to raise kids. A big house means more room for kids to have their own bedrooms, space to play, and a back yard to run around in safety. A car makes it a lot easier to ferry kids around to school, or soccer practice, or wherever. Cars also make it much easier to do large grocery shopping trips — try taking a week’s worth of food for a family of four home from the store on foot or on a bike and you’ll quickly understand.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It’s almost a cliche that people move to the city when they’re young — to jump-start their career, to party, to meet friends, to explore the world, to date around, and to find their spouse — and then move out to the ‘burbs once they settle down and have kids. The cliche is rooted in reality. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Instead of attacking suburbia, just make room for everybody</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Instead of treating the suburbs as some sort of hellish place that Americans’ car culture has exiled them to, urbanists should recognize that suburbs have real advantages that dense urban cores can’t easily replicate. Yes, too many Americans are pushed out to the ‘burbs by unaffordable housing. But a lot move there of their own free will, because they want a nice place to raise kids, enjoy a short quiet drive to work, and hang out with their friends in a big comfy house. It’s not the lifestyle for everyone, but it’s the lifestyle that a lot of people love and aspire to.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Which doesn’t mean we should ignore the real disadvantages of suburbia, either. Low-density sprawl is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9bc0478b-9988-403a-98b9-1fc71cf1eecc?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">very expensive to maintain</a><span>. It tends to make people </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f748ae27-a49c-4418-b1e7-64e2f6705697?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">less healthy</a><span>, because they walk less. It reduces variety among restaurants and brick-and-mortar retail outlets, because it’s harder to cater to niche tastes when you don’t have a critical mass of people nearby. Those tradeoffs shouldn’t be ignored. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Nor should we accept that the current suburban form is the optimal one. A lot of American urbanism has focused not on Manhattanizing urban cores, but on giving suburbs a few more of the benefits of cities — creating “gentle density” with rowhouses and duplexes and small apartment buildings, allowing retail in residential areas, adding bike lanes and commuter rail, and so on. This should all continue. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But it’s simply a mistake to frame the question of urban form as “Which is better, cities or suburbs?”. The answer is that </span><em>they’re good for different things</em><span>, and </span><em>they appeal to different sets of people</em><span>. Instead of fighting flame wars over whether the whole country should look like Manhattan or the Inland Empire, we should aim for </span><em>a country that has room for everyone</em><span>. We should build great city centers for the same reason we should build great suburbs — because Americans deserve to have great places to live, no matter what kind of place they want to live in. And I think these questions have the same answer.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>People keep comparing Platner’s rise to that of Donald Trump, but Platner reminds me of nobody so much as Hunter Biden: a substance-abusing egomaniac who sponged off his family, repeatedly obtained and abused the trust of people who really should not have given it to him, and somehow got laid a </span><em>lot</em><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I am attracted to men, so at a gut level, I get it — Platner and Hunter Biden both have sex appeal, at least when they are not heavily intoxicated. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ee22612e-8a60-4933-830d-efcf78dbab8b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">A lot of the Kennedys have been sexy, too</a><span>. These men have a kind of sex appeal that is a </span><em>problem</em><span>; it helps them get away with shit, and they end up hurting people, especially women. But importantly, the seductiveness these men exhibit is not solely sexual. They get women to sleep with them, but they attract both men and women and cause them to surrender their better judgment and make bad choices in a variety of contexts, including the voting booth. There is a personality type at work here — indeed, I would venture, there are </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/14d82cd3-62c4-4215-a399-192d0236eef4?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">cluster B personality disorders</a><span> at work — and it is important not to become entangled with this type, in politics or in life.</span></p><div The main fault in this episode lies with an electorate that ignored</span><strong> </strong><span>all the signs that </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d00b328e-8a0f-4c9d-9b88-c518d70031ca?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Platner might be bad news</a><span>, from his Nazi tattoo to his Reddit posts to his complete lack of achievements in life.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To me, the grimmest aspect of the public reaction to Platner’s implosion is the extent to which his erstwhile supporters appear surprised. Have they never encountered charming scoundrels in their personal lives? As Sean Trende notes, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/56da324d-009c-4cf2-a6f7-5480db9f0d0d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Platner is the figure that Andrea Dworkin tried to warn the left about</a><span>. Source: Trading Economics</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Oil prices did not, however, rise as much as many observers thought they would have to given the huge fraction of global oil supply — around 20 percent — that formerly passed through the Strait. And shipments through the Strait have never come close to fully resuming. So why was the price almost back down to prewar levels before this latest blowup?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Part of the answer is that the world found ways to reduce the impact of the Hormuz closure. Millions of barrels of oil a day literally bypassed the Strait via pipelines. Suppliers outside the Persian Gulf, including Venezuela, increased production. China sharply </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/dc52b4cc-4cd3-4a3b-b3d9-3796fcfc88d9?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">reduced its oil imports</a><span>. And a significant part of world oil demand was met by drawing down inventories.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There was, however, another factor: The effective price of oil </span><em>to consumers</em><span> — which is the price that matters for demand — rose a lot more than the crude oil prices one usually hears about. Even before the latest crisis that effective price remained far above prewar levels. And these continuing high prices to consumers kept oil demand low and hence depressed the demand for crude.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What do I mean by the “effective price” of oil? Consumers don’t burn crude oil. They burn products like gasoline and diesel that are refined from crude oil. As Javier Blas points out in a very useful </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f9e8cf26-93d7-4a17-86b9-e500304304fd?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Bloomberg article</a><span>, a rough rule of thumb is that every three barrels of crude are refined into two barrels of gasoline and one barrel of heavier distillates like diesel fuel.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Since there are 42 gallons in a barrel, this suggests that the effective price of a barrel of oil to consumers is 28 times the pump price of a gallon of gasoline plus 14 times the price of a gallon of diesel. style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As you can see, the price of oil to consumers rose substantially more than the </span><span>actual </span><span>price of crude — around $75 a barrel versus $45. This presumably led to a much larger fall in demand than one would have predicted from the price of crude alone. And effective prices to consumers were still far above </span><span>pre-war</span><span> levels even before the latest </span><span>round of </span><span>shouting-and-shooting between Trump and the IRGC began. The</span><span> higher effective</span><span> prices </span><span>to consumers </span><span>were holding global demand down even though crude prices were almost back to </span><span>pre-war</span><span> levels.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>W</span><span>hy are prices of gasoline and diesel so high compared with crude oil prices? As Blas explains, because there is a global shortage of refining capacity.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Some of this shortage reflects the loss of refined products that were formerly exported from the Persian Gulf. But a big factor now is the ongoing war between Russia and Ukraine.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Before that war began, Russia was a major exporter of refined petroleum products. But Ukraine’s astonishing mastery of drone warfare has enabled </span><span>this valiant </span><span>democracy to carry out an ever-more-effective strategic campaign against Russian energy infrastructure, above all its refineries. Russia not only can’t keep exporting gasoline and diesel fuel, it’s</span><span> now</span><span> facing major shortages (and huge gas lines) at home, and may </span><span>soon </span><span>be </span><span>forced to </span><em>import</em><span> refined products.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The result is, as I said, a global shortage of refining capacity</span><span>.</span><span> Blas suggests that around 10% of world refining capacity is now out of operation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And this shortage of refining capacity makes the collapse of the </span><span>jerry-rigged </span><span>deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz less relevant than one might have thought. To oversimplify, a true reopening of the Strait would have made more crude oil available to the global economy, but that wouldn’t have done the global economy much good in the short run, because </span><s>in </s><span>the world d</span><span>oesn’t</span><span> have the capacity to turn that crude into usable products.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Perhaps</span><span> that’s too glib. I think it’s fair to say that almost none of it is optimal.  </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Lenin said of the bureaucracy, “better fewer, but better.” When it comes to immigration, I don’t see it that way. We should try to be more selective, but we should also want more immigrants to come to the United States than ever. So while I agree that many of the current visa programs aren’t ideal, unlike Stephen Miller or Elon Musk, I don’t have my hair on fire about it. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What’s crazy, though, is that for how much conservatives rant and rave about immigration, the Trump administration isn’t even </span><em>seeking</em><span> legislative changes to American immigration law. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>They’ve enacted many consequential temporary changes, but the policy pendulum is just going to keep swinging, and they seem to genuinely believe the </span><em>current</em><span> situation is pretty bad. It’s possible that this is just a tactical error, but I think if you pay attention to the contrast between the apocalyptic rhetoric that rightists use on immigration and their lackadaisical attitude toward the legislative process, you also see the seeds of something more insidious: immigration as a </span><em>pretext</em><span> for abandoning democracy. </span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">The power of legislation</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Both fans and foes of Donald Trump are sort of grimly fascinated with the ways in which he’s wielded executive power, so much so that I think the significance of actual legislation he’s signed has become underrated. </p><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But consider this — 21st-century Democrats have been extraordinarily unwilling to raise taxes on anyone other than the super rich. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">There’s a one-way tax ratchet, and once a G.O.P. tax cut passes, Democrats are only willing to partially reverse it. As a result, even though almost no Democrats backed George W. Bush’s 2001 or 2003 tax cuts, almost all Democrats ended up supporting the extension of a majority of those tax cuts in 2010 and 2013. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The same thing happened with Trump’s 2017 tax cuts — the bill got zero votes from Democrats, but they were only willing to partially roll the cuts back. The 2025 Trump tax cuts were full of gimmicks like “no tax on tips” that Democrats didn’t vote for and wouldn’t have affirmatively enacted but aren’t going to want to repeal. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This isn’t a special feature of Trump or even of tax policy. No Republicans backed the insurance-market regulatory reforms that Democrats passed in 2010, but when Republicans tried to repeal them in 2017 it was hideously unpopular. Now they’ve landed where Democrats are on taxes: not even trying to repeal one of the main features of a bill they once unanimously opposed. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">All kinds of legislation tend to be sticky. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>On immigration, by contrast, Trump has just been governing through executive action. He really clamped down on irregular arrivals at the southern border. He also shut down Biden administration “parole” programs, whereby thousands of Haitians, Cubans, Nicaraguans, and Venezuelans </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e0967e25-7db9-43e9-9534-25d4e0c134e5?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">were able to enter the country legally</a><span> if they had qualifying sponsors in the United States. Trump has not made any new grants of Temporary Protected Status and has been yanking said status from groups that received it under previous administrations. Refugee resettlement has </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0dfdd147-199a-4603-ba57-42d642c1256f?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">been limited</a><span> to white South Africans. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">These are all meaningful policy changes, but a lot of them will be reversed the next time a Democrat is in office. The next Democratic administration will, I think (and hope), act with more decisiveness than Joe Biden on basic border security. But especially if they succeed at that, and thus don’t have a public opinion millstone around their neck, they’re almost certainly going to reverse course on these other Trump immigration actions. And when people come on Temporary Protected Status or parole and have kids on American soil, those kids will be American citizens. Even if the next Republican administration kicks those families out, the kids — as citizens — will have the right to return as adults. And because the American green-card system is heavily weighted toward family unification, those American citizens will be able to sponsor relatives for further immigration. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The only thing Trump has even </span><em>tried</em><span> to do to address conservative grievances about all this is issue an executive order purporting to end birthright citizenship. When the Supreme Court smacked that down, a bunch of conservatives threw a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5ac87052-b318-49a2-9b68-1a13ce7c84f6?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">demagogic hissy fit over absurd scenarios</a><span> to which the legal doctrine doesn’t even apply. </span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px style="text-decoration: none;">Subscribed</span></a></div></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>By passing laws that cut SNAP and Medicaid and reduce the federal revenue base, Republicans have made it very difficult for the next Democratic administration to do anything on the welfare state other than roll back Trump’s cuts. But it will be incredibly easy to </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/73c03449-cb8b-4dc5-9d1a-7ec6252dcb17?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">bring back Haitians to eat everyone’s pets</a><span>. </span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">An offer Democrats can easily refuse</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Of course, if Trump </span><em>did</em><span> try to change immigration law, he would find it quite difficult. The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025 passed because they were budget reconciliation bills. The 2025 law contained a ton of money for immigration enforcement because you can do that in a reconciliation bill. It did </span><em>not</em><span> contain any substantive changes to immigration law because you cannot do that in a reconciliation bill — which is also why the Biden administration was not able to deliver on its promise of a path to citizenship for millions of long-resident illegal immigrants. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So that’s an impasse. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One potential solution, of course, would be to change the filibuster rule so that immigration-policy changes can be made by majority vote. I’ve been an </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b15a47de-b6d4-46fa-9c08-db70a5566f42?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">advocate for filibuster abolition since at least 2005</a><span>. Instead, successive Congresses keep chipping away at it in incremental and creative ways. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I can’t predict where this will go, except to say that neither party seems particularly eager to change the filibuster specifically for immigration purposes. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This leaves the possibility of a bipartisan bill. When Joe Biden was president, he maintained for a while that only legislation could clean up the asylum mess. Republicans then demanded an asylum bill as a condition for delivering aid to Ukraine. Chris Murphy and James Lankford negotiated such a bill, but Donald Trump got wind of it and decided it would serve his interests for no bill to pass, so he pulled the plug. Then Republicans let Ukraine aid go through without the asylum bill attached. But then </span><em>Democrats</em><span>, who initially were only willing to do the bill because it was paired with Ukraine aid, realized it would be a good idea to do it. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">By that time, though, Republicans were unwilling. Biden then addressed asylum through executive action, and Trump has done the same. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Still, the old loosey-goosey asylum rules are on the books if any later administration wants to go back to them. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The Murphy-Lankford bill would have tightened those screws and also limited executive discretion on parole somewhat. I understand that restrictionists did not </span><em>love</em><span> this legislation because they thought it didn’t tighten the screws enough and they didn’t like the idea of letting Biden take a victory lap over a bill they felt was pretty lax. Still, they had all Democrats willing to do a restrictionist bill in exchange for nothing!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Trump could try to get something similar done if he wanted to. Or he could push for a bill that has tougher forward-looking measures but also offers Democrats more. Trump, for example, seems to have given up on trying to cancel the Obama-era Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program that gives de facto legal status to so-called Dreamers who came to the country illegally when they were underage. Democrats would like to give them permanent legal status and a path to citizenship. Perhaps in exchange for something like that, Democrats would be willing to make restrictionist changes in other areas. A bunch of Republicans now say they want to </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b445335c-aa1b-425e-95d1-5199f6bc4ca3?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">expand H-2A guest worker visas for farmworkers</a><span>, and they’re willing to make concessions around a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/04f230fa-d224-4d8e-b341-fec9b8003b4b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">path to citizenship for some illegal immigrants</a><span> currently working in agriculture. That latter idea is also a priority for many Democrats and could be part of a larger compromise. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I’ve tried over the past few years to ask Democrats what they actually want out of immigration policy and what their red lines are, and honestly they mostly seem very confused about it. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I think it’s possible that if Trump engaged in a serious legislative effort, he’d get something done. It’s also possible that he wouldn’t and Democrats would tie themselves to the mast of unreasonable demands. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">By declining to put forward a plan, though, he’s made it very easy for Democrats to say no to any durable policy changes. But we’re not going to find out whether a deal was possible, because Trump isn’t trying and he’s not taking criticism from anyone on the right for leaving a future Democratic administration free to reverse course. This is a bit weird as long as you accept that the parties are going to alternate in power. But perhaps some influential figures on the right don’t accept that. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">The immigration pretext</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Part of what’s happening here is that just as I often complain about </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/aeb5dc01-39a7-43c8-8900-358f9fbbece5?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">on the left</a><span>, a lot of conservative politics is fundamentally expressive. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Taxes are an exception. The well-connected people who pull the strings in Republican Party tax-policy circles really want lower taxes and they fight for that. But on immigration, what a lot of conservatives seem to want is to </span><em>get mad and complain</em><span> rather than actually do anything. Having the president write a memo purporting to overturn a Supreme Court precedent that’s more than a century old and then becoming enraged when that doesn’t work is not an actual attempt to alter immigration policy — it’s just getting mad. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Or perhaps it’s something more insidious. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In late June, I saw an </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8f40e82e-5a4f-47d5-93cb-58ea13502e9f?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Elon Musk post</a><span> endorsing a meme from the new right-wing movie “Citizen Vigilante.” The idea here is that you can’t just do immigration policy qua policy or treat disagreement about immigration policy as part of the normal give-and-take of politics. Instead, </span><em>before</em><span> tackling the immigrant menace, you need to destroy the domestic political power of the “traitors” who disagree with you. </span></p><div 16px;">If you reject both liberalism and democracy, that’s a pretty good reason to opt out of the legislative game and take over immigration! It’s also really bad. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I am well aware that there are </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b53b3da6-9793-4bc6-a0e1-3d6e70523838?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">swirling currents of illiberalism</a><span> on both sides of contemporary American politics. But I find this particular anti-liberal push from the right remarkable for a number of reasons: </span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Elon Musk is way richer and more influential than any individual actor on the left. </p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Prominent leftists tend to at least </span><em>pretend</em><span> to adhere to basic democratic norms and don’t typically fantasize openly about murdering their political opponents. </span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">The combination of high levels of expressed concern about immigration policy paired with total disengagement from the legislative process seems rampant on the right. </p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">There just really is some choosing to be done here. If American democracy is going to continue to exist, then people who want to see large changes made in immigration law need to either change the filibuster rule and accept that the opposition party will take advantage of these changes when it’s their turn to govern, or else engage in a bipartisan negotiation. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The good news, if you’re a conservative, is that the terms of a potential bargain have shifted to the right. If you look at </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2b2251ec-eccc-4e8c-a23e-7ee186a6e104?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Ruben Gallego’s immigration proposals</a><span>, for example, you’ll find a prominent Mexican-American politician willing to settle for less expansive legalization programs than the 2013 Obama deal plus a tighter approach to future flows. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Of course that was 2025, when Democrats were feeling underwater on the immigration issue. Trump’s actions since then have mostly served to generate public opinion backlash and make Democrats feel that the politics of the immigration status quo are survivable. That, again, is part of the reason why traditionally you try to pursue policy priorities through legislation to cement gains rather than just shove the pendulum around. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If all you want to do is delegitimize the constitutional order and entrench some kind of quasi-permanent kleptocratic oligarchy, though, the something. This is something. Therefore, we must do this.” — the Politician’s Fallacy</em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The other day, a friend asked me to add my signature to a statement called “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/19c5d678-7551-4c54-9ec2-065be1cb4c17?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">We Must Act Now: A Statement on AI’s Transformation of the Economy</a><span>”. A bunch of economists, including many famous and influential ones, have been signing it. Here’s the text of the statement:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><ol style="margin-left: 20px;margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>AI may become radically more powerful over the next 10 years.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>This could drive an unprecedented transformation of our economy, larger than the Industrial Revolution, but unfolding over a vastly shorter time frame. It could bring risks, including large-scale job displacement, as well as opportunities such as major gains in living standards.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Economists, policymakers and technology leaders must act now to understand the economics of transformative AI and to build the incentives, guardrails, and institutions needed to steer AI in a direction that complements humans and benefits society.</span></p></li></ol></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That’s it. That’s all it is. It doesn’t say </span><em>what</em><span> our action ought to be, only that “we must act”. There’s no appendix, no longer manifesto attached below. It just says AI is getting good, AI could be economically important, AI could take people’s jobs and/or make us a lot richer, and that we have to do </span><em>something</em><span> to make sure the AI age turns out alright. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But what </span><em>is</em><span> that something? What actual policies would I be recommending by signing this statement? None that I can see. It’s completely vague and unspecific. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This might seem like it makes the statement innocuous and bland (so why not sign it?). At some point, however, the authors may decide to release a </span><em>second</em><span> statement, with policy specifics. I’ll inevitably be associated with those ideas, even if I don’t sign the second statement. Relatively few people will pay attention to the difference between who signed only the first statement and who signed both. So by signing this first statement, I would essentially be giving my imprimatur to unknown policy proposals. I don’t want to do that. So I didn’t sign. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In fact, the existing statement, vague as it is, does contain at least one clue as to the kind of ideas that the authors will eventually come up with. At the end, it calls for us to “steer AI in a direction that complements humans”. I recognize this as the main idea in the book </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0d4aeba1-d584-42c4-a4d6-f7ca2363b80f?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Power and Progress</a><span>, by Daron Acemoglu and Simon Johnson. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In fact, not only did Acemoglu sign the statement, but it appears that the authors changed the text in order to get him to sign! </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b64c8e40-759b-40e4-9520-779820bd2358?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">He writes</a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span><span>Why did I sign this statement?…First, I had a hand in revising it, after the organizers reached out to me. I did not feel like I could sign the initial version…[M]ost importantly, I wholeheartedly agree with the ending: “to build the incentives, guardrails, and institutions needed to steer AI in a direction that complements humans and benefits society.”</span><br><br><span>This is what I have been arguing for over a decade now. Good AI needs to complement humans, and this requires a redirection, because the current focus on AGI is, in all but name, an agenda for displacing humans from meaningful work. That’s why steering AI must be a first priority.</span></span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So although Acemoglu doesn’t say which part of the final text he got to insert in exchange for his signature, it’s a pretty good bet that it’s the part about “steering” AI. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As it happens, I think “steering” AI is a </span><em>bad</em><span> policy idea. The first reason is that it’s basically impossible; </span><em>no one actually knows</em><span> how a technology will complement or substitute for human labor at the time they invent it. Inventors don’t know how their inventions will ultimately be used by businesses — and the more general-purpose a technology is, the less they know. Could James Watt, in 1765, have predicted most of the applications of steam power? Absolutely not. So he had no way of knowing whether the steam engine would ultimately create more jobs than it destroyed.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In fact, although AI might eventually be a big job-destroyer, right now it doesn’t seem to be. The employment rates for people age 20-24 and 25-54 are both just about the same as they were before ChatGPT ever existed:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: Kharazian</a></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is despite the fact that lots of people in the AI industry think their inventions are going to destroy jobs. So far they’ve just been wrong, and many of them are </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1819f4d4-ae49-4961-83e3-7415006e3320?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">feeling pretty astonished</a><span> right now. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Even when it comes to specific occupations, technologists are often startlingly wrong on the “complement or substitute” question. Geoffrey Hinton, one of the inventors of modern AI, famously predicted the end of human radiologists within a few years, only to see </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3e970db5-a4fb-467b-8321-9e8872958419?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">a boom in hiring and salaries for radiologists</a><span> when it turned out that AI actually </span><em>complemented</em><span> their skills.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So how the heck are businesspeople and inventors supposed to “steer” AI toward being complementary to human workers? They obviously couldn’t predict the labor market effects of the last round of AI — at least, in the short term. So why should anyone believe that technologists have the ability to purposefully invent different forms of AI with different labor market effects? </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The second problem with the idea of “steering” AI is the question of who does the “steering”. Acemoglu’s book, </span><em>Power and Progress</em><span>, never answers this question. Here’s what I wrote in </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/15c66f1f-5014-4d09-b880-68dfc727e1f4?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">my (very long) review</a><span> of that disappointing book:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Acemoglu and Johnson admit that “redirecting” the path of technological innovation is going to be an incredibly tall order…</span><span>[H]ow do we know in advance, </span><em>before a technology is invented</em><span>, whether it will increase or decrease the labor share?…Fundamentally, it still boils down to some sort of mandarins in a room somewhere — economists? government engineers? bloggers? — trying to assess the economic effects of a technology that </span><em>doesn’t even exist yet</em><span>…[T]his is probably an impossible task.</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Acemoglu himself has certainly not had a better record than the technologists when it comes to predicting the effects of AI on jobs. He wrote an empirical paper claiming that companies that buy robots tend to hire fewer workers, but this paper was </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d76f54f1-6c7c-4c8d-8c3b-57f84b146d74?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">contradicted by a very large number of follow-up studies</a><span>. And he wrote a theoretical paper claiming that AI wouldn’t do much to raise productivity, but that prediction was based on </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b4cfd466-a213-4ec7-a3b3-549e5bac8dd3?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">arbitrarily assuming away parts of his own model</a><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So any panel of wise mandarins that Acemoglu and his fellow-travelers assemble in order to “steer” AI technology is likely to have absolutely no idea what they’re doing. Here’s what I </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/27ab372a-c4bd-4d9e-8752-0b7bb7512c15?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">wrote about that idea</a><span> back in 2023:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">[I]f we were to set up a panel of experts and task them with deciding which lines of research and innovation to encourage and which to discourage in order to maximize jobs and wages, they would be operating purely on gut instinct and quasi-science-fictional supposition…[I]n practice, any panel or commission set up to speed up and slow down various types of AI will be simply adding noise to the innovation process, offering rewards and punishments essentially at random. That’s not good for the development of technology as a whole, since it introduces uncertainty into the innovation equation. But it’ll also be ineffectual in terms of actually protecting human workers.</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Three years later, having witnessed so many of the dire predictions of job destruction dashed on the rocks of reality, I see absolutely no reason to change my assessment. Acemoglu’s big idea — basically, to put him and his friends in charge of AI development — is not a good idea.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In fact, the surprisingly benign effect of AI on jobs so far calls into question the very notion that “We Must Act Now”. Yes, I agree that AI presents </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8fd348aa-55ad-4903-8df9-89588e2029c6?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">a very severe </a><em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8fd348aa-55ad-4903-8df9-89588e2029c6?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">security</a></em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8fd348aa-55ad-4903-8df9-89588e2029c6?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;"> threat</a><span>, and we must act on that. But on the economic front, it’s possible that </span><em>inaction is the right move</em><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Statistically speaking, we probably don’t live in the best of all possible worlds when it comes to AI’s economic effects. But we might be close enough that any large-scale attempt to interfere in AI development might leave average human workers worse off. There’s certainly plenty of historical precedent for that — collectivization of agriculture, Mao’s “backyard production”, and a bunch of other heavy-handed interventions in the development of an entire sector crashed and burned spectacularly. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It might be, in other words, that the AI we’re building now is </span><em>already highly complementary</em><span> to human workers, and that the best approach is not to “Act Now”, but to simply sit there and </span><em>do nothing</em><span>. Even the seemingly empty slogan of “We Must Act Now” might actually be wrong. Perhaps we mustn’t.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In any case, if the authors of the “We Must Act Now” statement add specificity to their policy proposals, I’ll consider signing it. But right now, the statement seems to hide some genuinely inadvisable Acemoglu-ism behind a screen of extreme vagueness.</p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px
